In summary, our research is concerned with
the preparation of NPs coated with antibodies, and the characterization of the NPs and their interaction with target cells.
the development of novel drug delivery systems for cancer therapy.
the development of novel nanomedicines based on the combination of NPs and mAbs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mAb-NP system is an effective tool for the targeted delivery of therapeutic agents to cancer cells.
the anti-HER2-NPs have a better potential for the treatment of HER2 positive cancers than anti-CD20-NPs for the treatment of CD20 positive B-cell lymphomas.
anti-HER2 NPS are more effective than anti-CD20 NPS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a method for the covalent coupling and targeting of antibodies onto nanoparticles.

we have shown for the first time that the targeting of tumor cells with mAb-NPs can be achieved by using two different targeting strategies: 1) binding of the mAb to a cell surface receptor and subsequent internalization of the mAb and the NP into the cells (anti-HER-2-NPs), 2) binding of the NP to a cell surface molecule but without internalization (anti-CD-20-NPs).
the choice of the mAb-target system defines the internalization of mAb-NP and the fate of the NPs after their binding on the cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of the ligand (mAb) defines the fate of nanoparticles (mAb NPs) after their binding to tumor cells.

the use of anti-CD20 Np for tumor targeting will not be efficient, as these NPs will not be internalized into the tumor cells, while anti-HER2 Nps are promising for the delivery of drugs to HER2 positive tumor cells.
mAb-NPs are promising for targeted cancer therapy.
